judgment.reasoning_summary: The polynomial P(x) is a sum of terms where each term's coefficient increases linearly with the power of x. For P(x) to have exactly one real root, it must change sign exactly once. This can be analyzed by considering the behavior of the polynomial as x approaches positive and negative infinity and by examining the derivative to find critical points. The polynomial will have exactly one real root if it is strictly increasing or decreasing over its domain, which occurs when the derivative P'(x) does not change sign. The derivative P'(x) = nx^(n-1) + 2(n-1)x^(n-2) + 3(n-2)x^(n-3) + ... + (n+1) is a polynomial of degree n-1. For P'(x) to not change sign, it must be either always positive or always negative. This happens when n is odd, as the leading term nx^(n-1) will dominate the behavior of the polynomial for large |x|. Therefore, the smallest positive integer n for which P(x) has exactly one real root is 1.
